facts.text: The rainbow lorikeet is a medium-sized parrot ranging from 25 to 30 cm long and weighing 75 to 157 g.
facts.quote: The rainbow lorikeet is a medium-sized parrot, with the length ranging from 25 to 30 cm (9.8 to 11.8 in), including the tail, and the weight varies from 75 to 157 g

facts.text: The rainbow lorikeet has a deep blue head, a greenish-yellow nuchal collar, green upper parts, and an orange/yellow chest.
facts.quote: The head is deep blue with a greenish-yellow nuchal collar, and the rest of the upper parts (wings, back, and tail) are green. The chest is orange/yellow.

facts.text: Males and females look identical, so DNA analysis of a feather is used to determine an individual's sex.
facts.quote: Males and females look identical, and surgical sexing by a veterinarian or DNA analysis of a feather is used to determine the sex of an individual.

facts.text: The rainbow lorikeet's tongue has a papillate appendage adapted to gathering pollen and nectar from flowers.
facts.quote: The end of the tongue is equipped with a papillate appendage adapted to gathering pollen and nectar from flowers.

facts.text: In Melanesia, rainbow lorikeets are important pollinators of coconuts, a very important food source for them.
facts.quote: In Melanesia, coconuts are very important food sources, and rainbow lorikeets are important pollinators of these.

facts.text: At Currumbin Wildlife Sanctuary, thousands of lorikeets gather in a huge, noisy flock around 8 am and 4 pm each day.
facts.quote: Around 8 am and 4 pm each day, the birds gather in a huge, noisy flock in the park's main area.

facts.text: Only the female rainbow lorikeet carries out incubation duties, and the species is mostly monogamous, often pairing for life.
facts.quote:
Incubation duties are carried out by the female alone.
Rainbow lorikeets are mostly monogamous and remain paired for long periods, if not for life.

facts.text: Thousands of rainbow lorikeets become paralysed each year in southeast Queensland, likely from the fruits of an unknown plant.
facts.quote: in southeast Queensland and northeast New South Wales, thousands become paralysed, most significantly, unable to fly or eat.
